prompt: Distribuidora Rio Pomba's credit request waits a day and six hours before an analyst claims it. Where is the instance during that wait?
hint: Nothing is running while it waits.

choices.text: In a server thread kept blocked until somebody claims the task
choices.why: No thread waits for days; a restart would lose it. The state is written down instead.

choices.text: In rows of the engine's own database, until a claim wakes it
choices.why: Right: the engine writes the position and the variables down and wakes the instance when a task is claimed.

choices.text: In the analysts' e-mail, as a message asking them to approve
choices.why: An e-mail goes to a person and is gone. A task goes to a group, waits, and shows its age.

choices.text: In Salesforce, which opened the request
choices.why: Salesforce started the instance through the bus; from then on the engine holds it.

prompt: The credit approval lived three days and three hours. What filled most of that time?
hint: Compare the solid marks with the dashed bars in the figure.

choices.text: The calls to the credit bureau and to SAP
choices.why: Both calls took three seconds together.

choices.text: The analyst's review of the numbers in the form, which took most of a working day
choices.why: The review took 25 minutes. The day and six hours before it was the task sitting unclaimed.

choices.text: Tasks waiting unclaimed in the analysts' list and then in the CFO's
choices.why: Right: a day and six hours for the analysts, a day and twenty hours for the CFO; the work itself took under half an hour.

choices.text: The engine working out which route the R$ 240,000 request had to take
choices.why: The decision is a comparison against R$ 150,000, made in an instant.

prompt: Put the life of Distribuidora Rio Pomba's credit request in order.
hint: It starts in Salesforce and ends in SAP.
items: Salesforce starts an instance through a flow on the bus
The engine fetches a bureau score and the open items in SAP
A credit analyst claims the task and reviews the request
Marcos approves a limit above R$ 150,000
The bus writes the new limit into SAP and the rep is told

prompt: An auditor asks who approved the R$ 240,000 limit. SAP's change record names a user. Why is that not the answer?
hint: Who wrote the value into SAP?

choices.text: SAP keeps no record of who changes a credit limit
choices.why: It does keep one, and that is the trouble: it names the account that wrote the value.

choices.text: Salesforce holds the approval, since the request was opened there
choices.why: Salesforce holds the request and the notice at the end, not the decision.

choices.text: The CFO approved by e-mail, so the answer is in his inbox
choices.why: He approved a task in his task list, and the engine recorded it.

choices.text: That user is the bus's technical account; who decided is in the engine's history
choices.why: Right: the analyst who claimed the task and the CFO who approved it are recorded only by the engine.

prompt: Match each family of tools to what it automates.
hint: Ask what each one replaces.

pairs.right: a screen a person would otherwise operate
a few steps between apps, over within hours
a long process with people, forms and inbox in one product
a long process run inside code your developers own

right_distractors: a file moved between two systems every night

prompt: RPA is fragile, yet the lesson calls a robot that retypes new farms into Coleta reasonable. Why?
hint: Three facts about Coleta.

choices.text: A robot costs less than an API in every case
choices.why: Cost is not the argument; with an API available, the API wins.

choices.text: The robot knows the onboarding process and checks what it types
choices.why: A robot knows the screen, not the business step behind it.

choices.text: Coleta has no API, its screen has barely changed in twenty years, and Coleta is being retired
choices.why: Right: no other way in, a stable screen, and a bridge with an end date.

choices.text: IBM BPM already calls Coleta directly, so the robot is a backup
choices.why: Nothing calls Coleta directly; a clerk retypes 23 fields today.

prompt: When a batch is quarantined in SAP, customer service wants a case opened in Service Cloud within minutes. Nobody decides anything on the way. What fits?
hint: Is there a person, and does anything wait for days?

choices.text: An integration or a short flow triggered by the event
choices.why: Right: data moving between systems in minutes, with nobody involved, is integration.

choices.text: A fourth process on IBM BPM, since the subscription is paid
choices.why: "The tool we already pay for" is the answer the lesson warns about; there is no person and no wait.

choices.text: A robot that watches the SAP quality screen for quarantined batches and types the case
choices.why: RPA is for a system with no other way in; SAP and Service Cloud both have interfaces.

choices.text: An open engine such as Camunda, inside a new service
choices.why: An engine keeps long cases open for people; this one is over in minutes.

prompt: A robot copies values into a SaaS screen. The vendor adds a new field above "amount". Which outcome is the worse one?
hint: One of them nobody notices.

choices.text: It stops with an error and somebody has to look
choices.why: That is the good case: the failure says so.

choices.text: It types into the wrong field and carries on
choices.why: Right: wrong data with no error is the failure nobody sees.

choices.text: The vendor's API refuses the robot's calls after the change
choices.why: A robot uses the screen, not the API; that is the point of RPA.

choices.text: It learns the new layout by itself and its next run is slower
choices.why: A robot follows the screen it was built against; it has no idea a field moved.

prompt: Suppose Serra Alta started 365 farm onboardings a year and each lasted 30 days. About how many would be open at any moment?
hint: Started per day, times how long each lasts.

prompt: Little's law predicts about 53 open instances, and the console shows 1,986. What does the gap say first?
hint: The estimate assumes that instances end.

choices.text: The business grew more than thirtyfold without anybody noticing
choices.why: The starts per year were known; the durations were what had gone wrong.

choices.text: The console counts every instance ever started, finished or not
choices.why: It counts active ones, and 1,925 of them were active only in name.

choices.text: Each process lasts a month or two longer than the table assumes
choices.why: Even three months each would give a few hundred, not nearly two thousand.

choices.text: Most are not live work: something keeps them from ending
choices.why: Right: 1,610 waited on a group with no members and 315 had failed; 61 were real.

prompt: Version 2 of farm onboarding adds a CAR step. Nobody migrates anything. What happens to the 18 farms halfway through?
hint: Which model were they started on?

choices.text: They stop at their current step until somebody adds the CAR step to them
choices.why: Nothing stops them; version 1 is still deployed and runs them.

choices.text: They finish on version 1, as they started, without the CAR step
choices.why: Right: each instance stays on the version it started on unless somebody moves it.

choices.text: The engine moves them to version 2 at their next step
choices.why: Moving them is a migration, and somebody has to decide to do it.

choices.text: The deployment is refused while version 1 has instances open
choices.why: Versions run side by side; that is how engines avoid this refusal.

prompt: Unless somebody migrates it, an instance keeps running on the version of the process it ___ on.
hint: Think of when it was created.

prompt: Which of these are true of the engine's history at Serra Alta? Choose all that apply.
hint: Two of them.

choices.text: It is the only record of who decided each credit limit
choices.why: Yes: SAP names the bus's account, not the person.

choices.text: It is copied into the warehouse every night with SAP's data
choices.why: It is copied nowhere, which is why nobody reports from it.

choices.text: Its tables are product internals, not an interface the vendor promises to keep
choices.why: Yes: so reports built on them are at the mercy of the next upgrade.

choices.text: Deleting a dead instance removes nothing an auditor would ask for
choices.why: A dead credit approval still holds who approved a limit; export before closing.

prompt: In 2019 the Fomento leiteiro team was folded into quality and its group emptied. Which defence would have shown the stuck farm onboardings within weeks?
hint: Nothing failed; something got old.

choices.text: Reading the engine's error log every morning
choices.why: A task waiting for a group with no members is not an error; the log stays clean.

choices.text: Restarting the engine each month to clear tasks that have waited too long
choices.why: A restart preserves every instance; that is what the database is for.

choices.text: An alert on the age of the oldest open task per group
choices.why: Right: the oldest Fomento task would have passed its limit about a month after the group emptied.

choices.text: Sending each task to a named person rather than to a group
choices.why: People leave too, and then the task waits for somebody who is gone.

prompt: A vendor says: "Our processes are drawn in BPMN, a standard, so you take them with you whenever you leave." What does that leave out?
hint: What is behind each box?

choices.text: Nothing: a BPMN file runs on another engine unchanged
choices.why: The file carries the shape; the behaviour lives in the product's own formats.

choices.text: The forms, scripts, integration services and variables behind the boxes
choices.why: Right: exporting the diagram exports the picture and leaves the behaviour behind.

choices.text: The layout of the diagram, which other modellers draw differently
choices.why: Layout is cosmetic; a rebuild costs the forms and scripts, not the positions of boxes.

choices.text: The licence key, which is embedded in every exported file
choices.why: Licensing is about the engine running, not about the export.

prompt: Which step in Joana's assessment buys the most safety for the least money?
hint: One person holds all the knowledge.

choices.text: Upgrading to Business Automation Workflow this year
choices.why: An upgrade is a project of its own, and Joana first asks IBM what it would cost.

choices.text: Re-implementing credit approval in Serra Alta's own code
choices.why: That is the first move out, and it costs months, not a hire.

choices.text: A second developer beside Vinícius
choices.why: Right: whatever is decided about the product, a single person who can change it is the plainest risk.

choices.text: Cancelling the subscription to fund the work
choices.why: Without support, a product nobody else understands gets riskier, not safer.

prompt: Which questions belong on Joana's list before buying a process suite? Choose all that apply.
hint: The list is about the engine and the contract.

choices.text: How are running instances handled when a process changes?
choices.why: Yes: side by side, migrated, or both.

choices.text: How fast can the vendor build our process in a demonstration?
choices.why: A demonstration shows the modeller, the cheapest part to own.

choices.text: Which number in our business does the licence metric follow?
choices.why: Yes: that number will change, and the bill with it.

choices.text: If we left in five years, what would we carry out, and in what format?
choices.why: Yes: the exit is priced before the entry.

choices.text: How many BPMN shapes does the modeller draw?
choices.why: Every serious modeller draws the notation; the cost is elsewhere.

prompt: The R$ 310,000 subscription got all the attention in Joana's first note. What reason does the lesson give for that?
hint: Where does each cost appear?

choices.text: It is the only cost on an invoice
choices.why: Right: forms, scripts, skills and history cost more and are printed nowhere.

choices.text: It is the largest cost of owning the suite
choices.why: The rebuild alone was estimated at seven months for two developers.

choices.text: IBM raises it every year under the contract
choices.why: The lesson says nothing of the kind; it is Serra Alta's figure, from its invoice.

choices.text: It is what every company pays IBM for the same product
choices.why: It says nothing about what IBM charges anybody else.

prompt: Denise argues that a fourth process on IBM BPM costs nothing extra, because the subscription is already paid. What is the strongest reply?
hint: Think about the day the suite is left.

choices.text: IBM licenses each process separately, so the bill rises
choices.why: The metrics the lesson names follow cores or users, not processes.

choices.text: BPMN has no shapes for a process that repeats every year
choices.why: A yearly process is a timer and an ordinary model; notation is not the obstacle.

choices.text: Re-qualification moves data between systems with nobody deciding, so it is integration
choices.why: A buyer and the quality team decide whether a supplier stays; that is a process with people.

choices.text: It adds forms, scripts and history to move one day, all on one developer
choices.why: Right: the marginal licence is small; what grows is what must be carried out, and the weight on Vinícius.

prompt: Put the steps of changing a process with instances running in order.
hint: Two populations, and the new version goes in beside the old.
items: Count the instances in flight and where they are waiting
Decide whether they drain on the old version or migrate
If migrating, map each deleted or merged step to a step of the new model
Deploy the new version beside the old one
Watch the last instance of the old version finish

prompt: Expected open instances = instances started per day × the average ___ of one instance.
hint: Little's law, 1961.

prompt: Why does Joana move credit approval first and farm onboarding last?
hint: Instance length, systems touched, and what else depends on it.

choices.text: Credit has the most forms, so moving it saves the most licence
choices.why: The licence follows cores or users, and the decision is about risk, not forms.

choices.text: Auditors care least about credit approval
choices.why: They care most: it is the only record of who decided each limit.

choices.text: Credit drains in a week and touches two systems; onboarding is tied to Coleta's future
choices.why: Right: four-day instances, Salesforce and SAP only; onboarding waits for lessons 7 and 13 to 15.

choices.text: Onboarding has the fewest instances open, so it is the safest to leave
choices.why: Onboarding had 1,610 stuck instances; it is last because of Coleta, not because it is small.
